payload.body: An equivalent-rectangular-bandwidth (ERB) is a human-made, frequency-dependent unit of filter bandwidth used to describe the frequency selectivity of the auditory periphery. It is defined as the width of a rectangular (flat) bandpass filter that would pass the same energy as a given auditory filter centered at frequency f. The standard empirical expression is ERB(f) = 24.7·(4.37·f + 1), with f in kHz and the result in Hz, so the equivalent width is about 104 Hz near 0.1 kHz and grows toward roughly 100·f at high frequencies — the auditory filter narrows relative to its center as f rises. Parameters: (1) the center frequency f (kHz); (2) the chosen fitting curve — the Glasberg & Moore (1990) expression is canonical, with alternative fits in the literature. Persistence mechanism: it persists as a standard psychophysically derived formula carried in the audiology and auditory-modeling literature (Glasberg & Moore 1990; Moore's auditory-filter and loudness work) and applied operationally to set the spacing and bandwidth of gammatone, bark, and auditory-filter-bank filters. Boundary: it is a unit of measure — a single number in Hz attached to a center frequency — not the auditory filter itself, not a signal's spectral bandwidth, and distinct from the generic signal-processing 'bandwidth' entry. The ERB formula ERB(f)=24.7·(4.37·f+1) is the standard parameterization used to set the bandwidth of auditory-filters to match cochlear selectivity. Removing ERB as a unit of measure would stop auditory-filters from being parameterized in the standard psychoacoustic way. The auditory-filter's accepted definition explicitly references ERB as its standard bandwidth rule.
